items.title: When the Saints Go Marching In
items.findings: No words in the file. A Christian spiritual about the day of judgement.
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a spiritual, as above.

items.title: Lucy Locket
items.findings: Kitty Fisher, named in the rhyme, was an eighteenth-century London courtesan, and the rhyme is said to begin as a joke about her. The words themselves are innocent.
items.suggestion: Keep as written; no change needed. A note for the teacher at most.

items.title: Au Clair de la Lune
items.findings: No words in the file. The later French verses (Lubin and the brunette) are mildly suggestive.
items.suggestion: Keep; if words are added, use the first verse only.

items.title: Canoinha nova
items.subtitle: Brazilian children's circle song — provisional plate reading
items.findings: Verse 1 (the new canoe that fell into the sea) is plain. Verse 2: "Pra sinh'Aninha cheirar": sinhá was the form of address enslaved people used for the master's wife or daughter. Verses 2 and 3 are courting verses (a carnation at the window; "Menina dos olhos grandes / Não olhe pra mim chorando").
items.suggestion: Teach verse 1, which is plain, once the plate reading is checked; leave verses 2 and 3 for a Brazilian educator, with a note on sinhá's history. Do not invent replacement words here.
items.source: Mário de Andrade, Ensaio sobre música brasileira (São Paulo: I. Chiarato & Cia., 1928), p. 36 (scan p. 46)

sourceUrls.label: Wikimedia Commons scan of the Ensaio, at scan page 46

dossier.function: roda (Brazilian children's circle song); Andrade prints three verses but does not describe the play action
dossier.elements: eight bars in 2/4; a compact rising-and-falling melody with one written G-sharp; three strophic verses
dossier.practice: sing the first verse at Andrade's crotchet 96; teach the Portuguese by echo before adding any accompaniment
dossier.honesty: provisional transcription from the 1928 plate; no harmony, percussion pattern, translation or game directions have been invented
dossier.licence: public domain source, first published 1928; Andrade died in 1945; the BBM/USP scan is marked public domain by Wikimedia Commons and IMSLP
dossier.respect: present it as a song collected in the former Federal Capital (Rio de Janeiro), not as a single definitive version for all Brazil
dossier.review: a Brazilian Portuguese speaker and children's-song or roda practitioner before promotion

items.title: Carry banana
items.subtitle: Jamaican ring tune
items.findings: "a Chiney banana": Jekyll explains it is a variety, the China banana ("a stout low kind which withstands wind"), but "Chiney" can be heard as a mocking word for Chinese people.
items.suggestion: Sing "China banana", Jekyll's own word for it in his note, and record the change in the N: line and in review-decision.
items.source: Walter Jekyll (ed.), Jamaican Song and Story (London: David Nutt, 1907), Project Gutenberg #35410 (music as MusicXML), no. XCIII, p. 196

sourceUrls.label: Project Gutenberg #35410: Jamaican Song and Story, with page images and the music

dossier.function: game: a chorus ring tune; the singers tease a girl carrying a bunch of bananas on her head, and "You find the banana?" is the signal to take a partner
dossier.elements: 3/4 waltz (Jekyll: Tempo di Valse); call "the gal over yonder" and the chorus "carry banana" answering; a raised A sharp leading to the B
dossier.practice: one in a bar; leaders sing the questions, the ring answers "carry banana"; a nine-hand bunch is market size, the China banana a stout low kind
dossier.honesty: arranged: melody and words as Jekyll printed them; the band plays a waltz under it
dossier.licence: public domain (published 1907; Project Gutenberg: for the use of anyone anywhere); notes converted from Gutenberg's MusicXML and checked bar by bar against its page image on 2026-11-10
dossier.respect: for everyone; "tief" is Patois for steal
dossier.review: a Jamaican culture bearer (a teacher of Jamaican folk song, or the Jamaica Memory Bank / Louise Bennett's recordings) before publishing

items.title: Soldier's Joy
items.findings: No words in the file. American sung verses mention morphine and beer ("twenty-five cents for the morphine").
items.suggestion: Keep as an instrumental with the note. It is the shorter of the two Soldier's Joy entries; keep both, or keep this one for the first tunes and the full Nottingham reel for later.

items.title: Greensleeves
items.findings: No words in the file. The old ballad's Lady Greensleeves is sometimes read as a woman of loose reputation; the tune is also the carol What Child Is This.
items.suggestion: Keep; no change needed.

items.title: Rama's lullaby
items.subtitle: Maratha lullaby
items.findings: A Maratha lullaby to the infant Rama as Vishnu ("It was Vishnu's self that was born on the lap of Kaushalya"), with devas strewing flowers: Hindu devotional words.
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a devotional lullaby, as above.
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 161, p. 66

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 66

items.title: Cuckoo's Nest
items.findings: No words in the file. "The Cuckoo's Nest" is also the title of a bawdy folk song in which the phrase is sexual slang.
items.suggestion: Keep the hornpipe as an instrumental; add a note "play the tune; the sung words are not for class", and leave the title.

items.title: Konpira fune fune
items.subtitle: Japanese game song
items.findings: No words in the file. The zashiki-asobi it belongs to is traditionally a drinking game at geisha parties in Kotohira: the player who hesitates drinks.
items.suggestion: Keep the tune and the hand game; reword the dossier from "party game" to "a party hand game from Kotohira" and teach the touching game only.
items.source: Nagai Iwai and Obata Kenhachiro (eds.), 1895, via Daisyfield.com transcription (Tom Potter, 2008, donated to the public domain)

dossier.function: game: a zashiki-asobi (party game) song from Kotohira, Kagawa; two players take turns touching a small stand in time, and a player who hesitates loses
dossier.elements: yo scale on G (G A C D E) ending on G; 2/4; the band holds an open fifth on G and plays taiko, hyoshigi and the chanchiki bell; no Western chord changes
dossier.practice: speeds up each time round in the game; the shamisen is the traditional accompaniment
dossier.honesty: arranged: the melody as Nagai and Obata printed it (via Daisyfield); the taiko-and-bell backing is ours, after festival min'yo
dossier.licence: public domain (Nagai and Obata, 1895; transcription donated to the public domain by Tom Potter, 2008)
dossier.respect: a party game song, for everyone
dossier.review: a Japanese culture bearer or a teacher of min'yo or koto before publishing

items.title: Lalishrita
items.subtitle: Tamil lullaby, from a phonogram
items.findings: A Tamil lullaby that lays the baby at the feet of Sriranga (Vishnu at Srirangam): Hindu devotional words (Fox Strangways's singing translation; stanza 2: "I lay thee there at Sriranga raja's feet, full sure of His tender care").
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a devotional lullaby so teachers can follow their school's guidance on religious songs.
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 155, p. 64

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 64

dossier.function: Tamil devotional lullaby, sung to a baby and placing the child in Sriranga's care
dossier.elements: flexible 6/8 phonogram transcription with triplets, grace-like runs, fermatas and rallentandos; C-centred melody spanning an octave plus a second
dossier.practice: Adagio, quarter note = 70 as printed; sing freely through the irregular bars and ornaments; the written range C4-C5 fits the conservative young-unison range, but the source's lyric underlay still needs checking
dossier.accompaniment: the plate prints only the vocal melody; begin unaccompanied, and treat the page's C drone as our optional pitch support, not documented Tamil practice
dossier.lyrics: Fox Strangways supplies an English singing translation, not the original Tamil words; stanza 2 is explicitly Hindu devotional text, so no classroom verse is approved until Tamil-language and Hindu-context review
dossier.honesty: historical-source transcription from a phonogram: melody and English singing translation follow Fox Strangways; tonic/drone, ABC handling of the five-note run and any backing are ours
dossier.licence: public domain source (A. H. Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan, 1914; author died 1948); four staves checked twice against p. 64 on 2026-11-09
dossier.respect: sacred/devotional reference to Sriranga (Vishnu at Srirangam); keep out of classroom publication until a Hindu/Tamil reviewer and the school context explicitly approve its use
dossier.review: Tamil speaker, Hindu educator or culture bearer, second plate reader and classroom teacher; all reviews still required

items.title: Little Sally Water
items.subtitle: Jamaican ring game
items.findings: Last verse: a mock wedding ("Now you married I give you joy, first a gal an' second a boy") ending "give her a kiss an' send her out". Mild, and common in playground versions.
items.suggestion: Keep the full text in the file as the source, and end the class version before "Now you married" (the ring game works without it).
items.source: Walter Jekyll (ed.), Jamaican Song and Story (London: David Nutt, 1907), Project Gutenberg #35410 (music as MusicXML), no. LXXXIX, p. 191

sourceUrls.label: Project Gutenberg #35410: Jamaican Song and Story, with page images and the music

dossier.function: game and dance: the ring game that gave its name to all "playing in the ring"; Sally crouches in the middle, rises, chooses a partner, and the two wheel
dossier.elements: two sections: an Andante call (rise, turn to the East and West) and an Allegro for the wheeling dance; English singing-game roots (Jekyll) sung in Jamaican style
dossier.practice: the tempo changes where the wheeling starts; the partner chosen becomes the next Sally Water
dossier.honesty: arranged: melody and words as Jekyll printed them; mento backing ours
dossier.licence: public domain (published 1907; Project Gutenberg: for the use of anyone anywhere); notes converted from Gutenberg's MusicXML and checked bar by bar against its page image on 2026-11-10
dossier.respect: for everyone; the last verse is a mock wedding, which some classes will skip
dossier.review: a Jamaican culture bearer (a teacher of Jamaican folk song, or the Jamaica Memory Bank / Louise Bennett's recordings) before publishing

items.title: Meu barco é veleiro
items.subtitle: Paraíba coco — provisional plate reading
items.findings: The second half is a courting line about complexion: "Eu amo a cor morena / A cor morena é que me ama" (I love the brown colour; the brown colour loves me). Morena is an everyday, affectionate word in Brazil, but like the "mulata" of Sambalele it ties a love song to skin colour.
items.suggestion: Keep it out of the published set until a Brazilian educator (and the coco reviewer the dossier names) says how classes sing it today; the tune itself is a good tonic-arpeggio study. Do not invent replacement words here.
items.source: Mário de Andrade, Ensaio sobre música brasileira (São Paulo: I. Chiarato & Cia., 1928), p. 75 (scan p. 85)

sourceUrls.label: Wikimedia Commons scan of the Ensaio, at scan page 85

dossier.function: coco; Andrade gives a short Paraíba verse and contrasts it with a longer Pernambuco call-and-response version
dossier.elements: 2/4; the Paraíba melody is restricted to the tonic-triad arpeggio, as Andrade explicitly notes; one short strophe
dossier.practice: learn the four Portuguese lines unaccompanied first; do not add a generic samba or bossa groove while the coco practice has not been reviewed
dossier.honesty: provisional transcription of Andrade's Paraíba plate only; the Pernambuco chorus and solo that follow on the page are not silently combined with it
dossier.licence: public domain source, first published 1928; Andrade died in 1945; the BBM/USP scan is marked public domain by Wikimedia Commons and IMSLP
dossier.respect: label the collected place and variant; do not present this four-line Paraíba version as the only form of the song or of coco
dossier.review: a Brazilian Portuguese speaker and a musician or culture bearer familiar with coco from Paraíba before promotion

items.title: Mīkhāhī labu?
items.subtitle: Do you want hot beetroot? (Persian folk song)
items.findings: Verse 1, line 2: "sarat havu biaram?" (shall I bring a second wife over your head?). Verse 2: "qeri-to doshak biaram?", Strettell: "A new mattress by thine to-night?" (bedroom innuendo). Verses 3 and 4: cigarettes ("sigar"). The refrain "na-na-i" is clean. The dossier wrongly says verses 2 to 4 are fine.
items.suggestion: Correct the dossier first. For class, sing only the first line ("mikhahi labu biaram?", shall I bring you hot beetroot?) with the refrain, or choose another of Fairchild's twelve songs after reading its words.
items.source: Blair Fairchild (coll. and arr.), Twelve Persian Folk-Songs (London: Novello, 1904), no. 4, pp. 15-17; English words by Alma Strettell; University of Rochester scan

sourceUrls.label: IMSLP: Twelve Persian Folk-Songs (Novello, 1904), Sibley Library (Rochester) scan

dossier.function: comic song: a suitor offers gifts (hot beetroot from the winter street-sellers, fireworks, a mattress, cigarettes) with a teasing refrain, "nā-nā-ī"
dossier.elements: 4/4, slow but gay; each verse two short phrases ending "bi-ār-am?" (shall I bring?) on B, then the refrain falling from C to E; notes E F G A B C, ending on E, close to the dastgah Shur; no Western harmony (Fairchild avoided it on purpose)
dossier.practice: a solo voice with the refrain answered loudly (forte); the band holds an open fifth on E with a frame-drum pattern of low dum and high tak
dossier.honesty: arranged: the melody and romanised words of verse 1 as Fairchild printed them; the frame-drum pattern and drone are ours and generic, not a tombak or daf rhythm a Persian musician has given us
dossier.licence: public domain (Blair Fairchild, Twelve Persian Folk-Songs, London: Novello, 1904; Fairchild died 1933, Alma Strettell 1939; University of Rochester, Sibley Music Library scan, "This item is in the public domain"); read bar by bar from the 400 ppi scan on 2026-11-10
dossier.respect: verse 1 jokes about bringing a second wife; verses 2 to 4 are fine for any class, and the refrain is the fun part
dossier.review: a Persian culture bearer (a speaker and a musician of Persian folk song) before publishing

items.title: Nirguna's lullaby
items.subtitle: Maratha lullaby
items.findings: No words under the notes; the title names Nirguna, the supreme being in Hindu thought, and the book's prose translation is a tired mother's lullaby (celestial carpenters made the cradle; my baby is not yet asleep).
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a devotional lullaby. Nothing in the words to change.
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 162, pp. 66-67

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 66

dossier.function: Maratha devotional lullaby; the translated prose is a tired caregiver singing while pulling the cradle string
dossier.elements: four-line 3/4 melody with repeats, triplet turns and Fox Strangways's wavy "squeeze" ornament; C final and a B-flat key signature whose B-flat does not occur
dossier.practice: no tempo is printed; quarter note = 80 is our lullaby estimate; the written A3-F4 range is low for conservative young-unison singing, and B-flat (+5 semitones, D4-Bb4) is the provisional rehearsal key
dossier.accompaniment: no accompaniment is printed; begin unaccompanied, and treat the C drone as our optional pitch support rather than documented Maratha practice
dossier.lyrics: no words are under the notes; the book gives only an English prose translation, so there is no approved singable text and no language pronunciation to teach
dossier.honesty: historical-source transcription: melody and prose meaning follow Fox Strangways; 3/4 barring, trial tempo, C drone and ornament rendering remain editorial interpretations named in the uncertainty note
dossier.licence: public domain source (A. H. Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan, 1914; author died 1948); four staves checked twice against pp. 66-67 on 2026-11-09
dossier.respect: the title and prose invoke Nirguna, the supreme being without attributes in Hindu thought; keep out of classroom publication until Hindu/Marathi context and school guidance explicitly approve its use
dossier.review: Marathi speaker, Hindu educator or culture bearer, second plate reader and classroom teacher; all reviews still required

items.title: Soldiers' Joy
items.findings: No words in the file. The same sung verses as the other Soldier's Joy (morphine and beer).
items.suggestion: Keep as an instrumental with the note. The arranger test uses this tune; it reads it from here while it is in review.

items.title: Sugar in the Gourd
items.findings: No words in the file. Sung versions of this old-time tune have a sexual double meaning.
items.suggestion: Keep as an instrumental with the same note: play the tune, not the words.

items.title: Sambalelê
items.subtitle: Brazilian roda
items.findings: Verse I: "Sambalele precisava e dumas boas lambadas" (Sambalele needed a good thrashing). The chorus sings "mulata" four times ("Pisa, pisa, pisa, mulata ... na barra da saia, mulata"), a word for a mixed-race woman with a colonial and racial history; verses II and III court a "mulata bonita" (how does one court? where do you live?).
items.suggestion: Keep it out of the published set until a Brazilian educator gives the words classes sing today. Choosing other verses is not enough, because "mulata" is in the chorus; do not invent replacement words here.
items.source: Mário de Andrade, Ensaio sobre a música brasileira (São Paulo: I. Chiarato, 1928), p. 38 (pdf p. 48), Wikimedia Commons scan

sourceUrls.label: Wikimedia Commons scan of the Ensaio, at scan page 48

dossier.function: roda (circle song and dance); sung in a ring with clapping, and still one of Brazil's best-known children's songs
dossier.elements: 2/4 with the Brazilian syncopation (semiquaver, quaver, semiquaver) and quaver triplets in the verse; a solo verse and a "Pisa, pisa" chorus that answers; D major, the verse reaching up to A, the chorus closing on D
dossier.practice: crotchet = 100 (Andrade); the ring claps and stamps on "pisa" (step); a samba de roda backing: surdo, ganza, tamborim, agogo, palmas and a strummed cavaquinho
dossier.honesty: arranged: the melody and words as Andrade printed them (Laranjal, Sao Paulo); the samba de roda band is ours, in the idiom
dossier.licence: public domain (Mario de Andrade died 1945; Ensaio sobre a musica brasileira, 1928; Wikimedia Commons scan, Public Domain Mark); read bar by bar from the scan on 2026-11-10
dossier.respect: the 1928 verse says Sambalele needs "a good thrashing" and calls a woman "mulata", a word with a colonial and racial history; many classes sing the chorus and other words, and a Brazilian teacher should choose the verse
dossier.review: a Brazilian culture bearer (a samba de roda or music teacher) before publishing

items.title: The ayah's song
items.subtitle: Hindostani song from the steamer
items.findings: No words. Fox Strangways calls the unnamed singer, a domestic worker and children's nurse on a colonial steamer, "an unmusical ayah"; our N: line now paraphrases his pitch observations without repeating that dismissal.
items.suggestion: Keep pending until a South Asian music/history reviewer checks the revised framing and the ethics of presenting an anonymous worker's melody; the requested human review has not occurred.
items.source: Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan (1914), Ex. 160, p. 66

sourceUrls.label: archive.org scan of The Music of Hindostan, at p. 66

dossier.function: undetermined air recorded from an unnamed ayah, a children's nurse, aboard a steamer; no classroom function is documented
dossier.elements: slow 3/4 C-centred air with printed slides at the close and half-close, irregular rests and a range extending to A3
dossier.practice: Adagio, quarter note = 80 as printed; sing or play with flexible slides; the written A3-G4 range is too low for conservative young-unison voices, and F (+5, D4-C5) is the provisional rehearsal key
dossier.accompaniment: no accompaniment is printed; begin unaccompanied, and treat the C drone as our optional pitch support rather than source practice
dossier.lyrics: no words are printed and the singer is unnamed; do not invent lyrics, language or translation
dossier.honesty: historical-source transcription: melody and printed grace-note slide follow Fox Strangways; tonic/drone, final-rest reading and any backing are our interpretations
dossier.licence: public domain source (A. H. Fox Strangways, The Music of Hindostan, 1914; author died 1948); both staves checked twice against p. 66 on 2026-11-09
dossier.respect: the colonial source dismisses the unnamed domestic worker's musicianship; paraphrase that account, foreground her anonymity and labour, and do not infer language or regional identity from the steamer setting
dossier.review: South Asian music historian or culture bearer, colonial-history/context reviewer, second plate reader and classroom teacher; all reviews still required

items.title: Jubilate Deo (round)
items.findings: A round on the Latin psalm Jubilate Deo (Psalm 100, "Rejoice in God"); no words in the file.
items.suggestion: Keep; label it a sacred round so teachers can follow their school's guidance on religious songs.
